name: Rosemary

soil.preferred_texture_seasoned: sandy, gritty, or gravelly with sharp drainage
soil.preferred_texture_beginner: Rosemary loves sandy, gritty soil that drains fast.
soil.tolerated_texture_seasoned: well-drained loam or shallow rocky soil
soil.tolerated_texture_beginner: Well-drained loam or rocky soil is fine as long as water runs through it.
soil.problematic_texture_seasoned: heavy, wet, or poorly drained clay that holds water around the roots
soil.problematic_texture_beginner: Heavy, wet clay is a problem because it holds water around the roots and rots them.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun. Rosemary is a Mediterranean subshrub that grows best in poor to average, dry ground; it performs poorly in heavy, flat, poorly drained clay. Overwatering and wet soil are the biggest causes of decline and death, so drainage matters more than fertility. On clay, plant on a raised bed or mound and add coarse material rather than piling on rich compost.
soil.preferred_description_beginner: Rosemary likes poor, dry, gritty soil and full sun. Rich, damp soil and heavy clay make it weak and rot-prone, so the goal is fast drainage, not fertility. If your soil is heavy, plant rosemary on a mound or raised bed and mix in coarse sand or grit so water drains straight through.

ph.note_seasoned: Rosemary does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, roughly pH 6.0 to 7.0, and tolerates a wider band from about 5.5 to 8.0. Extension herb guidance clusters around pH 6 to 7.5, and rosemary is adaptable as long as the soil drains sharply; getting drainage right matters far more than fine-tuning pH.
ph.note_beginner: Rosemary likes soil that is slightly acidic to neutral, about pH 6.0 to 7.0, and is not fussy within a fairly wide range. Do not worry too much about the exact number; good drainage matters much more to rosemary than pH does.

tip_seasoned: Treat rosemary lean and dry: full sun, gritty fast-draining soil, deep but infrequent water, and almost no feeding. Overwatering and soggy soil, not cold, are the top killers, though in zone 6 and colder you must also protect it from hard freezes or bring it indoors. Shape it with light tip pinching and harvest, and never cut back hard into the bare, leafless wood, which does not reliably resprout.
tip_beginner: The trick with rosemary is to not overwater it and to give it your sunniest, best-draining spot. Water deeply but only once in a while, and skip the fertilizer. Keep it shaped by pinching and snipping the tips, but do not cut way back into the old woody stems, because those usually will not grow back. In cold-winter areas, grow it in a pot so you can bring it inside before hard frost.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Rosemary has low fertility needs and is easy to over-feed. A little compost worked in at planting, or a single light application of a balanced fertilizer in spring, is plenty. Excess fertilizer pushes soft, lush growth that has weaker flavor and fragrance, flowers less, and is more prone to disease and winter injury.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Rosemary barely needs feeding. A little compost at planting is enough. Feeding it heavily gives you a lot of soft leaves with weaker flavor and scent, and a plant that is more likely to get sick or die back in winter.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: N/A. Rosemary is not fed to an N-P-K target; the aim is lean soil and minimal-to-no supplemental feed, so no fertilizer analysis applies.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: N/A. There is no fertilizer number to hit here, since the goal is to feed rosemary as little as possible.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: At most a little compost at planting, or one light spring feeding; often nothing at all.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A little compost at planting, and usually nothing after that.

companions.note_seasoned: Rosemary pairs naturally with other sun-loving, drought-tolerant, lean-soil plants that share its need for sharp drainage, especially fellow Mediterranean herbs like sage, thyme, and oregano that can all run on the same dry, waterwise schedule. As a small flowering plant it draws pollinators and beneficial insects such as bees and butterflies. Keep it away from thirsty, rich-soil neighbors that force the wet conditions which rot rosemary.
companions.note_beginner: Grow rosemary next to other plants that also like full sun and dry soil, such as sage, thyme, and oregano, so you can water the whole group the same light way. Its flowers bring in bees and helpful bugs. Keep it away from plants that need a lot of water, because that wet soil will rot your rosemary.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A fellow Mediterranean subshrub with the same full-sun, well-drained, low-water needs, so the two share one dry bed and watering schedule.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Sage (Salvia officinalis) is a close relative of rosemary with nearly identical culture: full sun, sharp drainage, low water, low fertility. Grouping the Mediterranean herbs lets you run one waterwise schedule and avoid the overwatering that rots rosemary. traditional/medium: shared-conditions co-cultivation, horticulturally well supported but not a measured pest or yield effect.

good_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low, drought-tolerant Mediterranean herb that thrives in the same lean, sharply drained soil and full sun.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Thyme shares rosemary's Mediterranean origins and dry, sunny, well-drained preferences, and its low mat form contrasts nicely with upright rosemary while asking for the same minimal water. traditional/medium: co-cultivation compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Another sun-loving, dry-soil Mediterranean herb that suits the same waterwise bed.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Oregano is a hardy, drought-tolerant Mediterranean herb with the same full-sun, lean-soil, low-water culture, so it co-cultivates cleanly with rosemary on one dry schedule. traditional/medium: shared-conditions compatibility.

good_seasoned.name: Lavender
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A woody Mediterranean subshrub with matching lean-soil, full-sun, sharp-drainage needs and a strong pollinator draw.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Lavender and rosemary are both woody Mediterranean subshrubs that want identical conditions (full sun, gritty fast-draining soil, little water) and both are strong pollinator plants, making them a classic dry-border pairing. traditional/medium: co-cultivation plus pollinator benefit.

good_seasoned.name: Cabbage and beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditional companion lore holds that aromatic rosemary planted near cabbages and beans helps mask them from some pests; useful as a beneficial-insect draw more than a proven repellent.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Long-standing companion-planting tradition places aromatic rosemary near brassicas and beans to confuse pests like the cabbage moth, and rosemary flowers genuinely attract bees and butterflies (Clemson). But the repellent effect itself is folk tradition, not a measured extension result, and cabbage and beans want richer, moister soil than rosemary, so site rosemary at the dry edge. traditional/low: real beneficial-insect draw, unproven repellent claim, and a soil-moisture mismatch.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Sage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Likes the same sunny, dry spot, so it grows happily next to rosemary.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same shared-conditions co-cultivation basis as the good_seasoned Sage entry. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Sage is one of rosemary's easiest partners because it asks for the same things: full sun, lean fast-draining soil, and not much water. That shared appetite is the real reason it works, since you can run the whole herb bed on one dry, waterwise schedule and avoid the overwatering that rots rosemary. Both are woody Mediterranean subshrubs, so they age and shape up similarly. Plant them in the same gritty, well-drained ground and resist the urge to pamper either.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Thyme
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Another dry-soil, full-sun herb that pairs well with rosemary.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Thyme. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Thyme and rosemary are natural bedfellows, both Mediterranean herbs that want full sun, sharp drainage, and little water. Low, spreading thyme fills in around upright rosemary and softens the front of a dry border, and the two never fight over water because neither wants much. Grow them in the same lean, well-drained soil and water sparingly once established.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Oregano
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Handles heat and dry soil like rosemary does.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Beginner-rendered bucket needing why_seasoned. Same basis as good_seasoned Oregano. traditional/medium.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Oregano is a tough, drought-tolerant Mediterranean herb that thrives on the same neglect rosemary does: full sun, poor lean soil, and minimal water. That makes it an easy companion that will not pull the bed toward the rich, damp conditions rosemary hates. Keep the soil gritty and well-drained for both, and water only when it dries out.

bad_seasoned.name: Basil and mint
bad_seasoned.timing: keep in a separate, wetter bed
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Basil and mint both want consistently moist, richer soil and frequent water, the opposite of rosemary's lean and dry regime; growing them in the same bed forces the wet conditions that rot rosemary. Mint is also aggressively spreading. Grow these thirsty herbs separately.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Basil and mint have genuinely opposite water and soil needs (moist, rich, frequent water) from rosemary's dry, lean, sharp-drainage ideal, and mint spreads aggressively; the conflict is a real cultural mismatch, so a bad pairing on shared-conditions grounds. traditional/medium.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling, dull or bronzed needles, and faint webbing, most common in hot, dry weather and especially on plants overwintered indoors in dry heat.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look dusty, dull, or speckled, sometimes with fine webbing, usually in hot dry spells or on a plant kept indoors over winter.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tiny sap-feeding mites that thrive in dry conditions. Dry indoor air over winter is a classic trigger, and drought-stressed outdoor plants are also vulnerable.
pests.cause_beginner: Very small mites that love dry air and dry, stressed plants. They flare up most on rosemary brought indoors for winter.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse plants with a strong stream of water regularly, raise humidity around indoor plants, and use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if numbers climb. Keeping the plant unstressed is the main defense.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the plant off with water regularly, and for indoor plants raise the humidity. Use insecticidal soap if there are a lot. A healthy, unstressed plant shrugs them off.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Discourage mites by spraying plants with a strong stream of water during dry spells and avoiding drought stress; indoors, give good light and some humidity and inspect plants before bringing them in for winter.
pests.prevention_beginner: Hose the plant down now and then in dry weather, and do not let it get badly drought-stressed. Before bringing rosemary indoors for winter, check it over for pests first.

pests.name: Aphids and whiteflies
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Occasional clusters of small soft aphids or tiny white flies on new growth and flowers, most often on stressed or crowded plants and on rosemary brought indoors.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Now and then, small soft insects or tiny white flies on the new growth or flowers, usually on stressed, crowded, or indoor plants.
pests.cause_seasoned: Sap-feeding insects that occasionally find rosemary. Outdoors, healthy plants in full sun rarely have trouble; indoor winter plants are more susceptible.
pests.cause_beginner: Small sap-sucking bugs that sometimes show up, mostly on indoor or stressed plants. Rosemary outdoors in the sun rarely has a problem.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse them off with water or use insecticidal soap if numbers rise. Improving airflow and removing nearby stressors usually resolves it.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, or use insecticidal soap if there are many. More air and less stress usually fixes it.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Give plants full sun, lean soil, good spacing, and airflow, and avoid overwatering. Vigorous, unstressed rosemary rarely attracts these pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep rosemary in full sun with room around it and do not overwater. Healthy plants rarely get these bugs.

pests.name: Spittlebugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Frothy white spit-like foam on stems in spring, with a small nymph hidden inside. It looks alarming but rarely harms an established rosemary plant.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Blobs of white froth that look like spit on the stems in spring, with a tiny bug hidden inside. It looks worse than it is.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spittlebug nymphs that shelter inside their own foam while feeding on sap. Numbers are usually low and the damage is mostly cosmetic.
pests.cause_beginner: Young spittlebugs hiding in the foam while they feed. There are usually only a few, and they do little real harm.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock them off with a strong spray of water if you find them unsightly. No treatment is needed for plant health in most cases.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If the froth bothers you, spray it off with a hose. You usually do not need to do anything else.
pests.prevention_seasoned: No specific prevention is warranted. Good spacing, full sun, and no overwatering keep rosemary vigorous enough to shrug off minor pests.
pests.prevention_beginner: Nothing special is needed. Giving plants room, sun, and not too much water keeps rosemary healthy enough to handle small pests.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing, wilting, browning tips, and dieback that does not recover with watering, often with a darkened, decayed crown at the soil line. It is the disease of concern for rosemary and is tied to wet soil and poor drainage.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Leaves yellow, tips brown, and the plant wilts and dies back even though the soil is wet, often with a dark, rotted spot where the stems meet the ground. This is the main thing that kills rosemary, and it comes from staying too wet.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Water mold pathogens (Phytophthora and related water molds) that thrive in saturated, poorly drained soil and attack the roots and crown. Overwatering and wet feet, not cold, are the underlying cause.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rot that takes hold when soil stays soggy and drains badly, attacking the roots and base. The real cause is too much water, not cold.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting; remove and discard affected plants. Focus entirely on prevention through drainage rather than rescue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fix, so pull out and throw away affected plants. The answer is preventing it with good drainage, not curing it.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and never let rosemary sit in wet ground. On clay, use a mound or raised bed, and space plants for airflow.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant in well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but rarely, and never let rosemary sit in soggy ground. On heavy clay, plant on a mound or raised bed and give plants room.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: A white powdery coating on foliage, favored by damp, still, humid air and crowded plants. It is most common on rosemary overwintered indoors and in humid regions, and is minor compared with root and crown rot.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white powdery film on the leaves, more likely in damp, still air or on crowded and indoor plants. It is a minor problem next to root rot.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi favored by poor air circulation and humidity. Crowding, low airflow, and stagnant indoor winter conditions raise the risk.
diseases.cause_beginner: A leaf fungus that likes damp, stuffy air with no breeze. Crowding and stale indoor air over winter make it worse.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow, thin crowded growth, and space plants; indoors, give good air movement and light. Remove badly affected foliage.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Give the plant more air and space, and for indoor plants keep some air moving. Pick off badly coated leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good air circulation is the main defense: space plants, site in full sun, avoid overhead watering, and do not crowd indoor winter plants.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep air moving around the plant: give it room and full sun, water at the base, and do not crowd it indoors over winter.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Deep and infrequent. Water regularly the first season until the plant is established, then taper to occasional deep soakings, letting the soil dry between waterings. Overwatering is the single biggest cause of decline.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply but not often. Give a new plant regular water until it settles in, then only water once in a while, letting the soil dry out in between.
watering.amount_seasoned: Enough to soak the root zone, then nothing until the soil has dried; mature plants in the ground need only infrequent deep irrigations.
watering.amount_beginner: A good soak when you do water, then let it dry out before the next one.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base and let the soil dry between waterings. Keep the crown and roots from staying wet, which invites root and crown rot; proper drainage is the real secret.
watering.method_beginner: Pour water at the base, not over the leaves, and let it dry out before watering again. Soggy soil is what makes rosemary rot.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing needles, browning tips, wilting or dieback of whole shoots, and a plant that fails despite watering signal too-wet roots and likely root or crown rot, not drought.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If the leaves yellow, tips brown, and shoots wilt or die back even though you are watering, the problem is almost always too much water. Soggy roots rot.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Established rosemary rarely shows true drought stress; brief wilting in extreme heat that recovers overnight is normal and not a reason to water more.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Rosemary almost never gets too little water once established. A little droop on a very hot afternoon that bounces back by morning is fine.

schedule_by_stage.rate: a soak to settle the plant, then let it dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: The first season is the only time regular watering matters: water a new rosemary regularly until it is established, then taper to occasional deep soakings. Water at the base and keep the crown and roots from staying wet against root and crown rot; proper drainage is the real secret.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Give a new rosemary regular water until it settles in, then only water once in a while, letting the soil dry in between. Water at the base and make sure it drains well.

schedule_by_stage.rate: infrequent deep soakings, then nothing until dry
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: A mature in-ground rosemary needs only infrequent deep irrigations, letting the soil dry fully between them; overwatering is the single biggest cause of decline. Water deeply, then nothing until the soil has dried, and keep the crown dry.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: An established rosemary needs only an occasional deep soak, letting the soil dry out fully in between. Too much water is the number one thing that kills it, so when in doubt, water less.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through dormancy rosemary wants next to no water; wet winter roots and crown invite rot, so ensure sharp drainage and do not let it sit wet.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: In winter rosemary needs almost no water. Wet winter soil rots the roots and crown, so make sure it drains and never sits soggy.

watering.method_note_seasoned: The most common way to kill rosemary is overwatering. When in doubt, water less.
watering.method_note_beginner: Remember: more rosemary dies from too much water than too little.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The first season after planting is the only time regular watering matters; taper off sharply once the plant is established.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Water fairly regularly the first year while it gets established, then back off a lot.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Nursery transplants are already hardened; set them out after the last spring frost. If you root your own cuttings, harden the rooted plants gradually before planting out.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you buy a plant from a nursery, you can put it straight in the ground after your last spring frost. There is no seed-starting step to worry about.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Rosemary is almost always started from a nursery transplant or from stem cuttings, not from seed. Seed germinates slowly and unevenly and can take about three years to reach a mature plant, and named cultivars do not come true from seed, so growers propagate them from cuttings. Take tip cuttings a few inches long, root them with warmth (bottom heat around 70 to 75°F), and they root in a couple of weeks. To grow from seed instead, surface-sow at about 70°F since the seed needs light, starting indoors roughly 10 weeks before the last frost; germination is slow and uneven and the seedlings size up gradually, which is why most growers still choose cuttings.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy, reliable way to grow rosemary is to buy a small plant or take a cutting from an existing one. Growing it from seed is slow and unpredictable, and seed-grown plants often do not match the parent, so most gardeners skip it. If you do want to try seed, surface-sow it and do not cover it, since the seed needs light to sprout, keep it warm around 70°F, and start indoors about 10 weeks before your last frost; expect slow, uneven germination.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering; rosemary must never sit in standing water.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A gritty, fast-draining potting mix, not a moisture-holding one.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in coarse sand or perlite so water runs straight through.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A coarse, free-draining potting medium; avoid peat-heavy moisture-retentive mixes.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Add coarse sand, perlite, or fine gravel to sharpen drainage.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out faster than the ground, so check the soil, but still let it dry between waterings and never leave the pot in a full saucer.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Container rosemary needs only a very light feed, if any; do not over-fertilize.

overwintering.approach_beginner: In cold-winter areas, grow rosemary in a pot you can move indoors for winter. Bring it in before the first hard frost, keep it in the brightest, coolest spot you have, water only when the soil is dry, and do not feed it until it goes back outside in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Where rosemary is not hardy, a container lets you overwinter it indoors. Bring it in before first frost to a bright, cool spot (it prefers cool nights, roughly 40 to 50°F, and days around 60 to 65°F); the hardest parts are giving it enough light, not overwatering, and not letting it dry out completely. Withhold fertilizer over winter and acclimate it outdoors gradually in spring.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Rosemary grows well in containers, which is the standard way to keep it in the coldest zones where it is treated as a bring-in plant, and to control the size of large upright types. Use a wide, free-draining pot and gritty mix, water only as the soil dries, and never let it stand in water. A trailing type like Prostratus is handsome spilling over a pot edge.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Rosemary does fine in a pot, which is handy if your winters are cold, since you can bring it inside. Use a wide pot with holes in the bottom and a gritty mix, let it dry between waterings, and tip out any water in the saucer.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Self-watering containers keep the medium too consistently moist for rosemary and promote root rot; use a conventional free-draining pot instead.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Skip self-watering pots for rosemary; they keep the soil too wet and the roots rot.

recommended.name: Tuscan Blue
recommended.hardiness_note: Perennial in about zones 8 to 10; not one of the cold-hardy types.
recommended.note: Vigorous upright type with thick stems, growing to 6 feet or more; a classic culinary and landscape rosemary.

recommended.name: Arp
recommended.hardiness_note: The hardiest rosemary, reliably surviving into zone 6 with good drainage and shelter.
recommended.note: The most cold-hardy cultivar, an upright plant 3 to 4 feet tall with light blue flowers; the pick for colder gardens.

recommended.name: Hill Hardy
recommended.hardiness_note: Second only to Arp for cold tolerance; a good choice for zone 7.
recommended.note: Also sold as Madalene Hill; a compact, dense, dark-green upright type, more cold tolerant than most.

recommended.name: Barbecue
recommended.note: Tall, stiff, straight upright stems, prized as skewers for grilling; reaches 4 to 6 feet.

recommended.name: Prostratus
recommended.hardiness_note: A trailing type that is less cold hardy, roughly zone 8; grow in a pot to overwinter in colder zones.
recommended.note: A low, trailing rosemary just 6 to 12 inches tall and 2 to 3 feet wide, ideal spilling over walls and containers.

recommended.name: Salem
recommended.hardiness_note: One of the more cold-tolerant selections, into about zone 7.
recommended.note: A compact, reliable culinary upright type well suited to herb gardens.

varieties.note_seasoned: Rosemary reaches the grower in two broad forms: upright types (Tuscan Blue, Barbecue, and the culinary standards) that make several-foot shrubs, and low, trailing types (Prostratus and similar) that spill over walls and pots. Because rosemary is cold tender, cultivar choice is really a hardiness choice in colder gardens: Arp is the hardiest, surviving into zone 6, and Hill Hardy and Salem are close behind for zone 7, while most other cultivars and the trailing forms are reliable only in about zones 8 to 10. For cooking, any of the upright green-needled types work well; for a container or a wall, choose a trailing form.
varieties.note_beginner: There are two main shapes of rosemary: tall upright types (like Tuscan Blue) that grow into shrubs, and low trailing types (like Prostratus) that hang over the edge of a pot or wall. In cold-winter areas the key is picking a hardy type: Arp is the toughest and can take zone 6, with Hill Hardy and Salem close behind for zone 7. Most other kinds only survive winter outdoors in warmer areas. For cooking, any upright green rosemary is great.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh-cut sprigs keep a few days standing in a glass of water on the counter, like cut flowers. For anything longer, refrigerate or dry them.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Fresh sprigs last a few days in a glass of water on the counter. To keep them longer, put them in the fridge or dry them.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Wrap fresh sprigs loosely in a slightly damp paper towel, seal in a bag, and refrigerate; they hold for one to two weeks.
storage.fridge_beginner: Wrap sprigs in a slightly damp paper towel, put them in a bag, and keep them in the fridge for a week or two.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole sprigs in a sealed bag, or strip and chop the leaves and freeze them in a little oil or water in ice-cube trays; frozen rosemary keeps for months and is best used in cooked dishes.
storage.freezer_beginner: Freeze whole sprigs in a bag, or chop the leaves and freeze them in a little oil in an ice-cube tray. Frozen rosemary keeps for months and works well in cooked food.
storage.notes_seasoned: To dry rosemary, cut sprigs before or at flowering, tie them in small bundles, and hang them upside down in a warm, dark, airy place; once dry, strip the leaves and store them whole in a sealed, opaque jar away from light and heat, crushing them only as you use them to preserve the oils. Both leaves and flowers are edible.
storage.notes_beginner: To dry rosemary, cut sprigs before it flowers, tie them in small bunches, and hang them upside down somewhere warm and airy. When dry, pull the leaves off and keep them whole in a sealed jar out of the light, crushing them only when you cook so they stay flavorful.

rotation.note_seasoned: N/A. Rosemary is a long-lived perennial that stays in place for years, so annual crop rotation does not apply. When replanting an old rosemary spot, choose a fresh, well-drained site to avoid carrying over soil-borne root rot.
rotation.note_beginner: N/A. Rosemary is not rotated like a vegetable because it is a permanent plant that stays put for years. If you replace an old one, pick a fresh, well-draining spot.

growth_stages.name: Plant out
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Set the nursery plant out after the last spring frost, in the sunniest, sharpest-draining spot you have. Space plants 24 to 36 inches apart, and on heavy or humid ground plant on a mound or raised bed.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After your last spring frost, plant the rosemary you bought in the sunniest, best-draining spot. Leave about 24 to 36 inches between plants for airflow.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A compact young plant with firm, needle-covered stems and roots filling the nursery pot, ready to set out once frost has passed.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A small bushy plant with green needle-like leaves and roots that hold the potting soil together when you slide it out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Loosen the rootball, set the crown level with the soil surface, and water in once to settle the roots. Do not add rich compost or fertilizer; rosemary wants lean ground.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Gently loosen the roots, plant so the top of the rootball is level with the soil, and water once. Skip the fertilizer and rich compost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Planted: type or cultivar, number set out, and the date.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down which rosemary you planted and when.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (year one)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first season after planting. Rosemary spends year one building roots, and a plant reaches full size in about three years.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first growing season. Your rosemary is busy growing roots and will not reach full size for a couple of years.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new green growth on the stem tips. The plant should be filling in bushy rather than stretching.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: New green needle growth filling in. You want it bushy and full, not tall and bare.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper to deep, infrequent watering. Pinch the growing tips to build a bushy shape, and harvest only lightly. Hold off on fertilizer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Pinch the tips to help it grow bushy, and only snip a little. Do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Establishment: planting-out date, watering taper, and any early pinching.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when you planted it and that you are watering less as it settles.

growth_stages.name: Growing and harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Through the warm season the plant pushes fresh green growth, and this is the main window for snipping sprigs. In mild climates leaf harvest continues nearly year round.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: During the warm season new green growth appears and you can snip sprigs freely. In mild areas you can harvest almost year round.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Soft green new growth at the stem tips, the best part for cooking and for cuttings.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fresh green growth on the tips, which is the tender part to cook with.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Snip sprigs from the soft green growth as needed, taking no more than about 20 percent at a time, and pinch tips to keep the plant bushy. Water deeply but infrequently.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip sprigs from the green tips as you need them, but do not take more than about a fifth at once. Pinch the tips to keep it full, and water deeply but not often.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Growing and harvest: harvest dates and any shaping done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you harvested and trimmed.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Rosemary flowers with small blue blooms, mainly late winter into spring in mild climates and later, into summer, in colder zones. Leaf flavor is strongest just before and during flowering.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Rosemary makes small blue flowers, usually in late winter or spring in warm areas and later where it is cold. The leaves taste strongest right around flowering.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small pale blue (sometimes pink or white) flowers along the stems, and busy bees. This is a good time to harvest for the best flavor.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Little blue flowers along the stems and lots of bees. It is a good time to cut sprigs for cooking.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Enjoy the flowers and the pollinators, and harvest sprigs for peak flavor. Keep watering deep and infrequent and do not feed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Enjoy the flowers and cut sprigs for the best flavor. Keep watering deeply but rarely, and do not fertilize.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bloom: first-open date and any harvest cuts taken.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it bloomed and when you cut sprigs.

growth_stages.name: Shape and light prune
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: After the main flush of bloom, lightly shape the plant and control its size by cutting into green, leafy growth. Never cut back into the bare, leafless wood, which does not reliably resprout.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: After it finishes its main bloom, trim to shape it, cutting only into the green leafy parts. Never cut down into the bare woody stems, because those usually will not grow back.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A plant that has finished its main bloom and could use shaping. Below the green growth are bare woody stems; those are your no-cut zone.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A plant done with its main flowers that has gotten a bit loose. Notice the bare woody stems lower down and do not cut into those.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Trim lightly into green growth to shape and size the plant, using the trimmings in the kitchen. Avoid a hard cut into old wood, and do not prune heading into a hard freeze.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Trim into the green growth to shape it, and use what you cut in cooking. Do not cut into the old wood, and do not prune right before a hard freeze.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Shape and prune: date and roughly how much removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Wrote down when you shaped it.

growth_stages.name: Winter (cold zones)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Rosemary is evergreen, but in cold zones growth stops for winter and the plant must be protected. Where it is not hardy, bring container plants indoors; wet soil and hard freezes, not the cold air alone, are what kill it.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Rosemary keeps its leaves but stops growing in winter. In cold areas it needs protection: bring potted plants inside, since a hard freeze or soggy soil will kill it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A plant that has stopped putting on new growth. Outdoors in mild zones it holds its green needles; in cold zones a tender plant left out will brown and die after a hard freeze.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A plant that has stopped growing. In mild areas it stays green; in cold areas a plant left outside will turn brown and die after a hard freeze.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: In hardy zones, stop watering and feeding and leave hard pruning for spring. In cold zones, bring container plants to a bright, cool indoor spot before the first hard freeze, water only when dry, and do not feed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: In warm areas, stop watering and feeding and save trimming for spring. In cold areas, bring potted rosemary inside to a bright, cool spot before hard frost, water only when dry, and do not feed it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Winter: date growth stopped and any protection or bring-indoors done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Noted when it stopped growing and any winter protection you added.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your plant-out window is open. Set the nursery plant in full sun in sharply drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants 24 to 36 inches apart. Skip rich compost and fertilizer.
notifications.body_beginner: It is time to plant your rosemary. Put it in a sunny, well-draining spot now that frost has passed, leaving 24 to 36 inches between plants, and do not add fertilizer.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to shape and harvest rosemary
notifications.title_beginner: Time to trim and harvest your rosemary
notifications.body_seasoned: Growth is active, a good time to harvest sprigs and lightly shape the plant. Cut into green, leafy growth only, take no more than about 20 percent at once, and stay above the bare woody base, which will not resprout.
notifications.body_beginner: Your rosemary is growing well, so snip sprigs and lightly shape it. Cut only into the green leafy parts, take no more than about a fifth at a time, and stay above the hard woody stems, which will not grow back.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your rosemary ready for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cold is coming. In hardy zones, stop watering and feeding and leave pruning for spring. In colder zones, bring container rosemary to a bright, cool indoor spot before the first hard freeze; a hard freeze or wet soil is the usual killer.
notifications.body_beginner: Winter is coming. In warm areas, stop watering and feeding. In cold areas, bring potted rosemary inside to a bright, cool spot before hard frost, since a hard freeze or soggy soil is what usually kills it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost on tender new growth
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Late frost on the new growth
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A late spring frost is forecast while the plant is pushing tender new growth. Protect newly set-out plants overnight and hold off on any planned shaping until frost has fully passed.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A late spring frost is coming while your rosemary has soft new growth. Cover any just-planted rosemary overnight and wait to trim until frost is over.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Humid heat raises rot and mildew risk
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot, humid weather raises rot risk
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A spell of humid heat is forecast, which raises the risk of root and crown rot and powdery mildew in muggy regions. Do not add water on rosemary's account, make sure it is not sitting wet, and keep airflow open around the plant.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Hot, sticky weather is coming, which can lead to root rot and powdery mildew. Do not give rosemary extra water, make sure it is not sitting in wet soil, and keep the area around it open and airy.

weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hard freeze is a danger to rosemary
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A hard freeze is forecast. Rosemary is cold tender and can be killed or badly damaged by a deep freeze, especially tender or trailing types. Move container plants under cover or indoors, and protect in-ground plants in marginal zones.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: A hard freeze is coming. Rosemary is not very cold hardy and a deep freeze can kill it, especially the tender or trailing kinds. Bring potted plants inside or under cover, and cover in-ground plants if you are in a borderline area.

transplant.text_seasoned: Plant rosemary lean and dry, not rich. Skip the compost-and-fertilizer routine other plants want, give it your sunniest, sharpest-draining spot, and on clay or in a humid region build a mound or raised bed. Wet, poorly drained soil is what kills rosemary.
transplant.text_beginner: Rosemary does best in poor, dry soil, so do not add fertilizer or rich compost. Give it your sunniest spot, and if your soil is heavy or your area is humid, plant it on a little mound or raised bed so water drains away.

transplant.text_seasoned: Space plants 24 to 36 inches apart for airflow. Good air circulation between plants is one of the simplest ways to head off the foliar disease rosemary can get in damp or crowded conditions.
transplant.text_beginner: Leave about 24 to 36 inches between plants. That space lets air move around each one, which helps prevent the leaf problems rosemary can get when it stays damp.

establishment.text_seasoned: Year one is about roots, not size. Water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep and infrequent. Pinch the growing tips to build a bushy framework; a plant reaches full size in about three years.
establishment.text_beginner: The first year is about growing roots. Water fairly often until it takes hold, then water deeply but less often. Pinch the tips so it grows bushy. It takes a couple of years to reach full size.

establishment.text_seasoned: Resist the urge to feed. Rosemary has low fertility needs, and over-fertilizing produces soft, lush growth with weaker flavor and fewer flowers. The same goes for water: more is not better.
establishment.text_beginner: Try not to feed it. Rosemary needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives you soft leaves with weaker flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Harvest little and often. Snip sprigs from the soft green growth as you cook, taking no more than about 20 percent of the plant at once, which both supplies the kitchen and keeps the plant bushy.
vegetative.text_beginner: Snip sprigs as you cook, but take no more than about a fifth of the plant at a time. Regular light cutting keeps rosemary bushy and gives you fresh leaves.

vegetative.text_seasoned: In hot, dry weather, hose the plant off now and then to discourage spider mites, and never let it sit drought-stressed for long stretches even though it is drought tolerant.
vegetative.text_beginner: In hot dry spells, spray the plant with water now and then to keep spider mites away. Rosemary is drought tolerant, but do not let it get badly stressed for too long.

bloom.text_seasoned: Leaf flavor and oil are strongest just before and during flowering, so this is the prime window to harvest for fresh use and for drying. Harvest in the morning once any dew has dried.
bloom.text_beginner: The leaves taste strongest right before and during flowering, so this is a great time to cut sprigs to use fresh or to dry. Cut in the morning after the dew dries.

bloom.text_seasoned: Leave some flowers for the bees. Rosemary blooms are a strong pollinator draw and, on English-clean unsprayed plants, both flowers and leaves are edible.
bloom.text_beginner: Leave some flowers for the bees, which love them. On your own unsprayed plants, the flowers are edible too, not just the leaves.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Shape rosemary by cutting into green, leafy growth only. It does not reliably resprout from bare, leafless wood, so never cut back hard into the old woody base the way you might a fast-renewing shrub.
cut_back.text_beginner: Shape rosemary by trimming only the green, leafy parts. It usually will not grow back from bare woody stems, so never cut hard into the old wood.

cut_back.text_seasoned: Time shaping cuts after the main bloom or in spring, not right before winter. A late-season hard cut leaves the cold-tender plant vulnerable to freeze damage.
cut_back.text_beginner: Do your shaping after it flowers or in spring, not right before winter. Cutting it back late leaves this cold-sensitive plant open to freeze damage.

dormancy.text_seasoned: In cold zones, bring container rosemary indoors before the first hard freeze to a bright, cool spot; it prefers cool nights around 40 to 50°F. Indoors the challenges are enough light, not overwatering, and not letting it dry out completely.
dormancy.text_beginner: In cold areas, bring potted rosemary inside before the first hard freeze and keep it in the brightest, coolest spot you have. Indoors, give it good light, do not overwater, but do not let it dry out completely either.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Pick a hardy cultivar if you want to leave rosemary outdoors in a cold-marginal zone. Arp survives into zone 6 and Hill Hardy into zone 7 with sharp drainage and a sheltered, south-facing site.
dormancy.text_beginner: If you want to leave rosemary outside in a borderline-cold area, choose a tough type. Arp can handle zone 6 and Hill Hardy zone 7 if the soil drains well and the spot is sheltered.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature plant supplies far more than a kitchen needs: sprigs can be cut continuously through the growing season, and nearly year round in mild climates, as long as you never remove more than about 20 percent at a time. Upright types yield the most cuttable growth once they reach full size in about three years.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One grown rosemary plant gives you more sprigs than you will likely use, and in mild areas you can cut from it almost year round, as long as you do not take more than about a fifth at once.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect only light harvests the first year; pinching tips to build a bushy framework pays off in later seasons.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Only harvest a little the first year. Pinching the tips helps the plant bulk up for bigger harvests later.
factors_seasoned: Plant age and size (full production at about three years)
Cultivar and form (large upright types yield more cuttable growth than trailing types)
Full sun and lean, sharply drained soil
Regular light harvest and tip pinching to keep growth green and productive

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves yellowing or the plant dying back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: With rosemary, yellowing, browning tips, and dieback almost always mean too wet, not too dry. Overwatering and poor drainage are the number one killer, leading to root and crown rot. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: For rosemary, yellow leaves, brown tips, and dieback usually mean too much water, not too little. Overwatering and soggy soil are the biggest killer. The plant is drowning, not thirsty.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut back on watering hard and fix drainage. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, water deeply but infrequently, and on clay or in humid regions use a mound or raised bed. Never let rosemary sit in wet ground.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Water much less and improve drainage. Use poor, well-draining soil in full sun, water deeply but only once in a while, and on heavy or wet ground plant on a mound. Never let it sit in soggy ground.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Browning or death after a freeze
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Rosemary killed or browned by cold
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Rosemary is cold tender. A plant that browned or died over winter was likely pushed past its cold limit: the species and most cultivars are reliable only in about zones 8 to 10, hardy types like Arp and Hill Hardy into zone 6 or 7, and a hard freeze below that range, especially on a tender or trailing type, is often fatal.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Rosemary is not very cold hardy. If yours browned or died over winter, it probably got too cold. Most kinds only survive winter in warmer areas, and even tough types have limits, so a hard freeze can kill it, especially the tender trailing ones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match the plant to your zone: choose a hardy cultivar (Arp for zone 6, Hill Hardy for zone 7) with sharp drainage and a sheltered site, or grow rosemary in a container and overwinter it indoors in a bright, cool spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick the right type for your winters. Use a tough cultivar like Arp or Hill Hardy with good drainage and a sheltered spot, or grow rosemary in a pot and bring it inside for the winter.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Bare woody stems or bland leaves
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A plant that has gone bare and woody at the base, or whose leaves have turned soft and bland, usually reflects too much feeding or water, or a lack of light harvesting. Over-fertilizing and overwatering drive lush growth with weaker flavor and fragrance, and rosemary that is never pinched or harvested gets leggy.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: If your rosemary has gone bare and woody at the bottom, or the leaves taste weak, it is usually getting too much food or water, or not enough trimming. Rich, wet conditions make soft, bland growth, and a plant that is never pinched gets leggy.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Stop feeding, water less, give full sun, and harvest regularly, always cutting into green growth and never into bare wood, which does not resprout. A badly woody, hollow plant is often better replaced than renovated.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Stop feeding it, water less, give it full sun, and snip it regularly, cutting only into the green and never the bare wood, which will not grow back. A plant that is already very woody is often best replaced.

failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Is rosemary safe for pets and cooking
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Good news on safety: rosemary is a well-established culinary herb, safe to eat in normal amounts and not considered toxic to cats, dogs, or horses. This is a friendlier profile than some ornamental herbs, so it is a sound choice around pets and children.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Rosemary is one of the safer herbs to grow. It is a normal cooking herb, safe to eat in usual amounts and not considered toxic to cats, dogs, or horses.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use only your own unsprayed plants for cooking, rinse harvested sprigs, and, as with any herb, keep pets from gorging on the plant even though it is not considered toxic.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cook only with your own unsprayed rosemary and give it a rinse. It is not toxic, but as with any plant, do not let a pet eat huge amounts.

open_findings.summary: Regional planting and bloom windows are MODELED (frost-resolved off the reused per-zone climate dates plus rosemary bloom phenology), not read from a rosemary-specific per-region extension planting chart, which does not exist for most of the 10 regions. Windows are generally-safe; tighten exact months at the variety-delta pass.

Cold-zone (northern_tier z3-6) grown_as=annual cells carry a MODELED first-summer bloom window; no T1 source gives a calendar-month first-year bloom for a container/replant rosemary set out after spring frost, and many rosemary plants bloom little in their first cold-zone season. Bloom timing there is a frost-resolved derivation; harvest of leaves (the real use) is continuous through the warm season.

Humid z10/z11 (fl_peninsula, hawaii_tropical) modeled as perennial-marginal: rosemary is genuinely grown there but is prone to root/crown rot and powdery mildew in humidity and needs excellent drainage or raised beds; UF/IFAS supports year-round Florida culture with freeze protection in colder areas. The reliably-perennial in-ground case in deep-humid lowland is under-sourced. Community-correction invited.

Judgment calls / modeled scalars: hardiness_zone_min=7 (species/most cultivars are z8 per NCSU/WI, hardy Hill Hardy z7, Arp z6; 7 chosen as the hardy-cultivar-inclusive reliable floor, driving the grown_as flip); hardiness_zone_max=10 (NCSU 10b); spacing 24-36 in (PSU 2 ft plus large upright sizes); productive_lifespan 10-15 yr and pH preferred 6.0-7.0 modeled from clustered guidance (NCSU lists acid <6.0 as an outlier); germination_temp 70F nominal (rosemary is propagated by cutting/transplant, not seed). Storage fridge/freezer methods are standard kitchen practice; only the drying claim is T1-cited.

Companions are TRADITIONAL/low-to-medium: fellow Mediterranean herbs (sage, thyme, oregano, lavender) on shared-conditions co-cultivation grounds; the cabbage/beans pest-repel pairing is folk tradition with a real beneficial-insect draw (Clemson) but an unproven repellent claim and a soil-moisture mismatch. No rosemary-specific companion trial in a read T1 source.

mid_atlantic z7 credits NC State with rosemary's "zone 7 to 8" hardy floor, but NC State's Plant Toolbox gives Salvia rosmarinus as 8a-10b, read from raw bytes 2026-07-31. The NUMBER is sound and is not in question: 7 is our own hardy-cultivar-inclusive floor per rosemary_pilot_finding_004 ("Hill Hardy z7, Arp z6", with the species itself noted as z8 per NCSU), and it matches rosemary.hardiness_zone_min = 7. It is the CREDIT that overstates, since NC State does not publish 7. Same defect shape as the mid_south UAEX credits removed 2026-07-31, but in a different region and so out of that hunt's scope. Needs its own ruling: either drop the NC State credit as mid_south's was dropped, or restate the sentence as our own cultivar-inclusive judgment.

plantings.label: establishment
plantings.synthesis_note_seasoned: Region-constant arms span the zone range. Rosemary is set out as a nursery transplant or rooted cutting, in the coldest zones only after the last spring frost and in mild zones in fall or late winter to spring. Bloom is frost/phenology-resolved (small blue flowers, late winter into spring in mild climates, later in cooler zones), not read from a planting-date table; the per-zone display windows are computed per zone. Where rosemary is not hardy, the coldest zones are grown as annual / bring-in container plants (MSU, UMN).
plantings.synthesis_note_beginner: These cover the whole region. Plant rosemary after your last spring frost in cold areas, or in fall to spring in mild areas. It flowers in late winter or spring in warm zones and later where it is cooler, and in the coldest zones you grow it for the season or in a pot you bring indoors.

plantings_provenance.note: plant_out + bloom arms are frost/phenology-resolved per zone then spanned across the region. Bloom phenology anchor: rosemary flowers late winter into spring in mild climates (PSU), spring into summer in cooler zones (NCSU). Regional month windows are MODELED, not from a rosemary-specific per-region planting chart (open finding).

3.grown_as_note_seasoned: Annual or container. Zone 3 is colder than rosemary's reliable hardiness (about zone 7 to 8), so it is grown as a single-season plant or, better, kept in a container moved to a bright, cool, protected spot for winter and set back out after frost. Hardy cultivars such as Arp can overwinter in a very sheltered, sharply drained zone 6 microclimate, but this is not the reliable default.
3.grown_as_note_beginner: Rosemary usually will not survive a zone 3 winter in the ground. Either grow it for one season or, better, keep it in a pot you move somewhere bright and protected for the cold months, then set it back out in spring. The tough cultivar Arp can sometimes make it through in a sheltered spot.
3.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Too cold to overwinter reliably in the ground here, so grow rosemary as an annual or in a container moved indoors for winter. Set plants out only after the last spring frost; the season ends at the first hard freeze.

The bloom window is a MODELED first-summer derivation (a mature container plant set out in spring can flower in summer); no T1 source gives a first-year cold-zone bloom month, so this is the weakest-sourced part of the cell. description_seasoned: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) is a woody evergreen Mediterranean subshrub in the mint family, grown mainly for its aromatic, needle-like culinary leaves and secondarily for its small blue flowers. It comes in upright forms that reach several feet and low trailing forms that spill over walls. Unlike hardier culinary perennials such as sage and thyme, rosemary is relatively cold tender: it is reliably perennial only in mild zones (roughly zone 7 or 8 and warmer, with the hardy cultivar Arp pushing into zone 6), and in colder regions it is grown as an annual or overwintered indoors in a pot. It wants full sun, lean sharply drained soil, and little water; overwatering and wet, poorly drained soil, not cold alone, are its most common killers.
description_beginner: Rosemary is an evergreen shrubby herb with fragrant, needle-like leaves and small blue flowers. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it loves sun and hates wet feet. You grow it mostly for the leaves, which you can snip year round in mild climates. It is less cold hardy than sage or thyme: it lives outdoors year after year only in warmer areas (about zone 7 or 8 and up), and in cold-winter places most people grow it in a pot and bring it inside for the winter. Give it full sun, fast-draining soil, and go easy on the water, since too much water is the fastest way to kill it.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Rosemary is grown for its leaves, and in mild climates you can snip fresh sprigs almost year round. For the strongest flavor and oil, harvest sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, just before or as the plant begins to flower. Cut individual stems above a leafy node to encourage bushy regrowth, and do not remove more than about 20 percent of the plant at any one time. For drying, cut sprigs before or at flowering, then hang them in small bundles in a warm, airy place and strip the leaves once dry.
harvest_ready_beginner: You grow rosemary for the leaves, and in mild areas you can snip sprigs almost any time of year. For the best flavor, cut sprigs from the soft green growth in the morning, especially just before it flowers. Snip stems just above a leafy joint so the plant grows back bushy, and take no more than about a fifth of the plant at once. To dry it, cut sprigs before or during flowering, hang small bunches somewhere warm and airy, and strip the leaves off once they are dry.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Rosemary is relatively cold tender for a woody herb. The species and most cultivars are reliably perennial only in about zones 8 to 10, and hardy selections such as Hill Hardy push into zone 7 while Arp is the hardiest, surviving into zone 6 with good drainage and a sheltered spot. Below that, in roughly zone 6 and colder, rosemary is grown as an annual or, better, kept in a container and moved to a bright, cool, protected place for winter. This is the opposite of hardier culinary perennials like sage and thyme, which overwinter outdoors much farther north.
hardiness_notes_beginner: Rosemary is less cold hardy than most herbs. It lives outdoors year after year mainly in warmer areas (about zones 8 to 10), and a few tough types like Hill Hardy and Arp can handle zone 7 or even zone 6 with shelter and good drainage. In colder places, grow rosemary in a pot and bring it inside for the winter, since it will not survive a hard freeze in the ground the way sage or thyme can.
year_one_notes_seasoned: In the first year, focus on root establishment: water regularly until the plant is settled, then taper toward deep, infrequent watering. Shape the young plant with light tip pinching to build a bushy framework, and harvest only lightly. A seed-grown plant takes about three years to reach full size, which is why rosemary is almost always started from a cutting or a nursery plant.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about getting the roots going. Water fairly regularly until the plant is established, then cut back. Pinch the tips to help it grow bushy, and harvest only a little the first season. Rosemary is slow from seed, so most people start with a small plant or a cutting.
soil_prep_seasoned: Choose the sunniest, best-draining spot you have. Rosemary wants lean, gritty, sharply drained ground, so work in coarse sand or grit on heavy soil rather than piling on rich compost. On clay or in humid regions, plant on a mound or raised bed so water drains away from the crown.
soil_prep_beginner: Pick the sunniest spot with the best drainage. If your soil is heavy, mix in coarse sand or grit so water runs through fast, and skip the rich compost. On clay or in a humid, rainy area, plant rosemary on a little mound or raised bed.
bloom_time_beginner: Rosemary has small blue flowers (sometimes pink or white). In warm areas it usually flowers in late winter and spring; in colder places it blooms later, in spring or summer. The flowers are a nice bonus for pollinators, but you grow rosemary mostly for the leaves.
bloom_time_seasoned: Rosemary blooms with small blue, and occasionally pink or white, flowers. In mild-winter climates it flowers mainly from late winter into spring, roughly January through April, and may rebloom; in colder regions it flowers later, in spring into summer. Bloom is a secondary feature, since rosemary is grown chiefly for its leaves, but the flowers are a strong draw for bees and other pollinators.

dormancy_window.note_seasoned: Rosemary is evergreen, but in zones with real winter cold its growth stops for the season. In hardy zones, hold off on watering and feeding and leave any shaping for spring. Where rosemary is not hardy, bring container plants to a bright, cool, protected indoor spot before the first hard freeze; it is a hard freeze or persistently wet soil, not the mere presence of cold, that usually kills it.
dormancy_window.note_beginner: Rosemary keeps its leaves through winter, but in cold areas it stops growing. In mild zones, just stop watering and feeding and save trimming for spring. In cold zones, bring potted rosemary inside to a bright, cool spot before hard frost, since a hard freeze or soggy soil is what kills it.

pollination.notes_seasoned: Rosemary is self-fertile and needs no pollinizer partner; it is grown for its leaves, not fruit, so no cross-pollination planning is required. Its flowers are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators.
pollination.notes_beginner: You only need one rosemary plant, and it does not need a partner plant. Bees love the flowers, but that is a bonus for your garden, not something the plant needs.

pruning_window.note_seasoned: Shape rosemary and control its size after the main bloom, or in spring, by cutting into soft green growth only. Rosemary does not reliably resprout from bare, leafless wood, so never cut hard into the old woody base. Regular light harvesting doubles as pruning and keeps the plant bushy; avoid a hard cut heading into a hard freeze.
pruning_window.note_beginner: Trim rosemary to shape it after it flowers, or in spring, cutting only into the green leafy growth. It usually will not grow back from bare woody stems, so never cut into the old wood. Snipping sprigs as you cook keeps it bushy, but do not cut it back hard right before winter.
